newsitem.title: HUNGARY: FOCUS - Hungary minister to revamp farm policy.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Hungary minister to revamp farm policy.

text.p: Hungary's agriculture minister presented on Friday a long-awaited draft of the country's medium-term farming policy as farmers' groups threatened a wave of protests.

"Despite its present crisis...Hungary's agriculture had a foreign trade surplus of $2 billion last year," Frigyes Nagy said, adding that the new ten-year plan was put together in a very short time and would need improvements.
"It is certain to contain mistakes and there is room for improvement," Nagy said about the programme.
Hungary's Socialist Party promised a comprehensive overhaul of the country's ailing agriculture before coming to power in the summer of 1994.

The announcement of the plan comes after a series of blockades by central Hungarian farmers protesting over increased social security and tax burdens. Other farming organisations said they could resort to similar steps in the near future.
Hungary's biggest farmers union appealed on Friday for talks with the government to overhaul Hungary's agriculture and threatened protests if talks are refused.
-- To set overall budget for farming subsidies, regional and environmental development at 2.5 percent of the GDP.
-- To increase agricultural exports to between $6 billion and $7 billion within ten years from the current annual $3 billion.
-- To achieve an annual three to 3.5 percent agricultural growth rate.
-- To shift the focus of farming subsidies towards the producers from the current system which concentrates on export subsidies.
-- To implement a market-based price system, guaranteeing farmers a return while keeping the price rises within acceptable limits.
-- To improve the agricultural credit system in order to promote much-needed investments.
-- To re-regulate land ownership, without permitting foreigners to own land.
Nagy said the government plans to open a wide-ranging debate on the plan, involving all interested parties.
He said current tensions between farmers and the government would not be an obstacle to the debate.
However, several farmers' associations have already complained that the ministry did not consult them when drafting the new document.
Nagy said the government plans to have the final version of the plan ready by the end of April and hopes to eventually turn it into a bill
He added that for such a bill to become possible some 30 other laws would need to be created or amended.
